title: WHAT SHOULD MARRIED CHRISTIANS NEVER JOKE ABOUT?
paragraphs: WHAT SHOULD MARRIED CHRISTIANS NEVER JOKE ABOUT?
Some Jokes Last Five Seconds. The Wound They Leave in a Marriage Can Last for Years.
Everybody laughed.
Except her.
Her husband had just told the story again—the embarrassing one.
The one about something she had trusted him enough to confess in private.
The table erupted.
Someone nearly spit out their drink. Another person slapped the table. Her husband looked pleased with himself because the punchline had landed perfectly.
She smiled too.
At least, her face did.
Under the table, her hands tightened.
Nobody noticed.
On the drive home, he finally asked, “What’s wrong?”
“Nothing.”
But something was wrong.
Because sometimes the most painful sentence in a marriage begins with four innocent-sounding words:
“I was only joking.”
And sometimes the person who promised to protect your heart discovers exactly where it is tender—and then uses that tenderness to entertain a room.
That is why Christians need to ask a question deeper than, “Can married couples joke about this?”
We need to ask:
“Does the way I joke with my spouse look like Jesus?”
Because Scripture is not against laughter.
God is not threatened by joy.
“A joyful heart is good medicine” (Proverbs 17:22).
Ecclesiastes says there is “a time to laugh” (Ecclesiastes 3:4).

Jesus Himself used startling imagery, irony, exaggeration, and unforgettable verbal pictures. The Christian marriage was never intended to feel like two frightened people living under a permanent cloud of religious seriousness.
Laugh together.
Be ridiculous together.
Have inside jokes.
Tease each other affectionately when both of you genuinely enjoy it.
Grow old enough together that you can finish each other’s stories and still laugh at the stories you have heard a hundred times.
But understand something:
Not everything that produces laughter produces love.
And laughter is never permission to violate the commands God has already given us about our words.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:4 about speech that does not belong among God’s people, including what many English translations render as “crude joking.” The Greek word is εὐτραπελία—eutrapelia.

The word can carry the idea of clever or witty speech, but in Paul’s immediate context it is associated with speech that has become morally inappropriate, shameful, or indecent. Paul does not condemn every clever joke. He contrasts degrading speech with thanksgiving.
That distinction matters.
The biblical question is not simply, “Was it funny?”
The biblical question is, “What did the joke do?”
Did it honor?
Did it humiliate?
Did it protect?
Did it expose?
Did it strengthen intimacy?
Did it turn something sacred into entertainment?
Did your spouse laugh because it was genuinely funny—or because everyone was watching and laughing was less painful than admitting you embarrassed them?
There are places in your spouse’s heart where comedy should enter carefully.
And there are some things Christian husbands and wives should refuse to turn into weapons disguised as punchlines.
Do not casually joke about divorce as though covenant abandonment is entertainment.
“I should’ve married someone else.”
“I’m trading you in.”
“One more argument and I’m filing for divorce.”
“Maybe my next husband will listen.”
“Maybe my next wife will actually cook.”
People laugh.
But the heart remembers.

Marriage in Scripture is covenantal, not disposable. Jesus takes marriage with profound seriousness in Matthew 19:4–6, pointing back to creation and declaring that husband and wife become “one flesh.”
The Greek expression is σὰρξ μία—sarx mia—“one flesh.”
Not two competitors temporarily sharing an address.
One flesh.

This does not mean every mention of divorce is sinful, nor does it erase the difficult biblical and pastoral questions surrounding abuse, abandonment, adultery, separation, or divorce. Those circumstances require truth, wisdom, safety, pastoral care, and sometimes professional or legal help.
But repeatedly threatening the covenant for comedy is something else.
Imagine building a house with someone and periodically joking that you might burn it down.
Eventually, they may stop sleeping peacefully inside it.
The same principle applies to adultery.
Be extraordinarily careful about jokes suggesting that you want someone else sexually or romantically.
“Your sister is looking good.”
“If he asked me out, you’d better watch yourself.”
“That actress is my real wife.”
“I only married you because she rejected me.”
Maybe everyone understands the joke.
Maybe your spouse even laughs.
But marriage is not merely a legal arrangement. It is a place where emotional and sexual exclusivity should be cultivated and protected.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage should be held in honor and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
Jesus goes even deeper in Matthew 5:27–28, addressing lust at the level of the heart.
So why would a Christian repeatedly make entertainment out of the very betrayal Scripture tells us to guard against?
Faithfulness should feel safe in your marriage.
Not fragile.
Not negotiable.
Not something your spouse has to compete for.
And never use your spouse’s body as a comedy routine.
Weight.
Age.
Hair loss.
Wrinkles.
Sexual performance.
Infertility.
Pregnancy changes.
Physical disabilities.
Medical struggles.
Features they already dislike about themselves.
There is a world of difference between affectionate teasing shared by two secure people and repeatedly targeting an insecurity because you know it gets laughs.
Your spouse gave you access that strangers do not have.
You know where they are insecure.
You know what happened in childhood.
You know what their former partner said.
You know what they see when they stare too long into the mirror.
You know what makes them feel unwanted.
That knowledge makes you powerful.
Christian love asks what you will do with that power.
Proverbs 12:18 says that reckless words can pierce like a sword, while the tongue of the wise brings healing.
A sword does not become harmless because the person swinging it is smiling.
Read that again.
A sword does not become harmless because the person swinging it is smiling.
Some spouses have become experts at stabbing lovingly.
They insult, then grin.
They expose, then laugh.
They belittle, then say, “You’re too sensitive.”
They wound, then make the wounded person feel guilty for bleeding.
That is not the tenderness Scripture calls husbands and wives toward.
Ephesians 4:29 gives Christians a radically different standard for speech: our words should build others up according to their needs and give grace to those who hear.
Grace.
Even in humor.
Especially at home.
Your spouse should not have to develop thicker skin just to survive your personality.
And please—do not turn private sexual intimacy into public entertainment.
There are things a husband knows about his wife that belong inside the sanctuary of their covenant.
There are things a wife knows about her husband that should never become material for the group chat.
The bedroom should not become tomorrow morning’s comedy content.
Your spouse’s private fears, sexual vulnerabilities, embarrassing moments, deeply personal disclosures, past trauma, failures they confessed to you, and struggles entrusted to you deserve discretion.
Love does not merely ask, “Is this technically true?”
Love asks, “Was this mine to tell?”
Proverbs 11:13 contrasts gossip with the trustworthiness of someone who keeps confidence.
There is something breathtaking about being married to someone who knows the ugliest chapter of your story and makes you feel safer because they know it—not more exposed.
That is intimacy.
Your spouse should be able to hand you something fragile without wondering whether you will eventually hand it to an audience.
And never joke about abuse, violence, coercion, or terror in a way that normalizes them.
“I’m going to kill you.”
“She needs a good slap.”
“I keep him in line.”
“He knows what happens when I get angry.”
Christian marriage is not permission for domination, intimidation, or cruelty.

Colossians 3:19 tells husbands to love their wives and not be harsh with them. First Peter 3:7 commands husbands to live with their wives with understanding and honor. Ephesians 5 places Christian marriage beneath the enormous shadow of Christ’s self-giving love.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε—agapate—from ἀγαπάω, agapaō.
Whatever debates surround the nuances of Greek words for love, Paul makes his intended meaning unmistakable by giving us the model:
Christ.
He gave Himself.
That destroys the fantasy that biblical headship is a license for humiliation, fear, or selfish control.
Jesus does not stand over His bride looking for vulnerabilities He can exploit.
He gives Himself for her.
Christian marriage therefore keeps returning to one terrifyingly beautiful question:
Does the way I treat my spouse resemble the way Christ loves His people?
That includes our jokes.
And there is another kind of humor that can quietly poison a marriage: contempt.
“My husband is basically another child.”
“My wife never stops talking.”
“You know husbands. They’re useless.”
“You know wives. They’re crazy.”
It becomes socially acceptable because everyone recognizes the stereotype.
But your husband is not “men.”
Your wife is not “women.”
This is the person whose hand you held while making promises before God.
When contempt becomes entertainment, disrespect becomes easier.
Then resentment becomes normal.
Then tenderness becomes awkward.
Then one day two people can sleep inches apart while living emotionally miles away.
It rarely happens all at once.
Sometimes marriages bleed through paper cuts.
One sarcastic comment.
One public embarrassment.
One private insecurity turned into a punchline.
One comparison.
One “joke” about another woman.
One “joke” about another man.
One “joke” about divorce.
One “joke” about sex.
One “joke” about failure.
Then another.
Then another.
Until somebody stops telling you what hurts because telling you has become dangerous too.
But this is where the Gospel interrupts the story.
Because perhaps while reading this, you did not think about what your spouse has done to you.
You thought about what you have done to your spouse.
You remembered their face.
That dinner.
That argument.
That joke.
That secret.
That moment everyone laughed.
And suddenly you remember that your spouse did not.
What do you do now?
Not defensiveness.
Not, “But I didn’t mean it that way.”
Not, “You joke about me too.”
Not, “Everyone knew I was kidding.”
Not, “You need to stop being so sensitive.”
Repent.
That word frightens people because we have reduced repentance to religious humiliation.
But biblical repentance is an invitation to turn.
The New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance, carrying the sense of a changed mind and turning expressed in a changed direction.
Repentance says:
“I see what my words have been doing.”
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“I will not hide behind humor.”
“Please forgive me.”
And then repentance produces fruit.
The joke stops.
The secret stays private.
The flirting disguised as humor ends.
The public humiliation ends.
The contempt ends.
The threats end.
You begin learning how to make the person you married feel safe in your words again.
Maybe you are the wounded spouse.
Perhaps you have laughed publicly and cried privately.
Perhaps everyone thinks your husband is hilarious, but you know what it feels like to be the material.
Perhaps your wife knows exactly which insecurity will silence you.
Perhaps “I was joking” has been used so often that you have begun wondering whether you are simply too sensitive.
Your pain should not automatically be dismissed merely because somebody else laughed.
At the same time, every awkward joke is not abuse, every insensitive comment is not evidence of a doomed marriage, and spouses must leave room for misunderstanding, forgiveness, maturity, and growth.
Christians should resist both extremes.
We should not call every imperfect sentence abuse.
And we should not call cruelty humor merely because someone laughed.
The Gospel gives us something better than both hypersensitivity and hardness.
It gives us truth wrapped in grace.
Jesus exposes sin without abandoning sinners who come to Him.
That is the heartbeat of the Christian story.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met Thomas.
The woman caught in adultery stood beneath the weight of public shame, and Jesus neither celebrated her sin nor surrendered her to condemnation. He called her toward a different life.
The cross itself announces something astonishing:
Your worst moment does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why there is hope for the husband whose tongue has been cruel.
There is hope for the wife whose sarcasm became a weapon.
There is hope for the marriage that has accumulated years of little wounds.
There is hope for the couple who has forgotten how to speak gently.
Not because words do not matter.
They matter enormously.
But because Jesus Christ is still in the business of transforming people.
You may not be able to retrieve every sentence you have spoken.
You cannot walk back into every room and catch every joke before it leaves your mouth.
You cannot erase every memory.
But through Christ, you can become someone who speaks differently tomorrow.
Confess your sin to God.
Confess specifically to your spouse where appropriate.
Ask forgiveness without demanding immediate emotional recovery.
Listen when they tell you what your words have done.
Do not argue with their wound.
And then begin rebuilding.
Slowly.
Tenderly.
Consistently.
Let your spouse discover that their weakness is safe with you.
Let them discover that their body is safe with you.
Let them discover that their history is safe with you.
Let them discover that their failures are safe with you.
Let them discover that the marriage covenant is not something you threaten whenever you need a punchline.
Then laugh.
Please laugh.
Laugh until your stomach hurts.
Laugh about the burnt dinner.
Laugh about getting lost on vacation.
Laugh about the ridiculous thing you both misunderstood.
Laugh about the harmless quirks you both genuinely enjoy teasing each other about.
Laugh about growing older together.
Build a home filled with joy.
But make sure the laughter leaves both people standing.
Because Christian humor should never require the sacrifice of your spouse’s dignity.
Before you make your husband the punchline, remember who he is.
Before you embarrass your wife for applause, remember who she is.
Not your content.
Not your target.
Not your emotional punching bag.
Not your comedy prop.
Someone made in the image of God.
Someone you promised to love.
Someone whose heart has been placed unusually close to your hands.
Handle it accordingly.
And if this article exposed something in you, resist the temptation to immediately send it to your spouse as ammunition.
Read it again for yourself first.
Ask Jesus:
“Lord, what needs to change in me?”
Maybe the most Christlike thing you do tonight will not be winning an argument about whose jokes are worse.
Maybe it will be walking into the room, sitting beside the person you love, and saying:

“I realize some of the things I’ve called jokes have hurt you. I’m sorry. I don’t want my humor to cost you your sense of safety with me. Will you forgive me? And will you help me understand where I need to change?”
That conversation may not fix everything tonight.
But grace often begins with somebody finally telling the truth.
And if your marriage needs prayer, there is no shame in simply commenting, “pray for us.”
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become reminders that Christian marriages are filled with real people who need real grace from a real Savior.
Supporting a ministry is not a requirement for earning God’s favor, proving your faith, or glorifying God—Christians glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
Take it home.
Take it into your marriage.
Take it before Christ.
Because perhaps the question was never merely, “What should married Christians never joke about?”
Perhaps the deeper question has always been:
“Does the person who knows me most intimately experience more of Christ because of the way I speak to them?”
Your marriage does not need two perfect people.
It needs two people who keep bringing their imperfect hearts to a perfect Savior.
Two people willing to repent.
Two people willing to forgive.
Two people learning when to laugh and when something is too sacred to become a joke.
Two people discovering that grace does not merely forgive what happened yesterday.
Grace teaches us how to love differently tomorrow.
And remember this:
The mouth that once made your spouse feel small can, surrendered to Jesus, become the mouth that spends the rest of your marriage reminding them they are deeply loved.
